description: What the application itself may call once the launcher has handed the window over to it. The launcher serves the application from the backend it started, at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/, and picks that port at runtime: 8732 when it is free and an arbitrary free port otherwise. Tauri classifies any such address as a REMOTE origin, because a local origin is only the Tauri protocol or a configured frontendDist URL, and this build's frontendDist is a directory. Without this file the application window is a remote origin with no capability naming it, so every command it invokes is refused by the access control list and the controls that depend on those commands do nothing at all. Seven of the nine application commands, and deliberately not the launcher-shell set, so no shell or process PLUGIN permission is granted here. That count said four of six for two releases while the list below held six entries, which is worth recording because a description nobody recounts is how a grant grows without anybody deciding to grow it. That is not the same as granting no shell surface, and it should not be read that way: open_app_in_browser reaches the OS opener, as open_external_url does. What bounds it is that the caller cannot choose the destination. The scheme and host come from the launcher's own resolved app_url, and build_local_url in src/main.rs accepts a caller-supplied path only when it starts with a single slash, is not protocol-relative, contains no scheme separator and contains no backslash; anything else falls back to the bare base URL. So the worst this command does is send the OS browser to a page on the server the launcher resolved. That sentence used to end in loopback and no longer can, because app_url may now name a server somewhere else; where THIS list applies it is still a loopback one, since a window served from anywhere else matches no pattern here and is refused every command in it. open_external_url and reveal_path_in_os are the two that take a caller-supplied destination, and they are the ones to think hardest about before adding anything beside them. open_external_url bounds itself by scheme: only http, https and mailto, so a crafted href cannot name a local program, and there is no shell on the way to the opener for a tail to run in. reveal_path_in_os bounds itself by place and by kind. The path is canonicalised and must resolve inside the data folder this launcher's backend stores files in, so a page cannot name a system folder or a network share, and the opener is always handed a DIRECTORY, a file's parent rather than the file, so nothing here launches a program by extension and an executable dropped into the workspace is not a way to run code from a page. It exists because the file manager's Open in OS button called the shell plugin directly, which this list refuses, so the button did nothing at all and the refusal reached users as a raw access control message in a bug report. The answer to that was a narrow command, not a shell grant. On the two server-choice permissions, which is the question this file exists to answer honestly: this list applies ONLY to http://127.0.0.1, which is a server the launcher itself resolved and started or attached to, and it does NOT apply to a server whose address a user typed into the settings, which is granted nothing at all and is refused every command here. The worst case for the loopback grant is a hostile process on this machine that bound a candidate port and answered the attach probe convincingly enough to become the origin; such a process is by definition already running as this user, and the setting these commands write is a plain JSON file in this user's own home folder, so it could write that file directly and the grant hands it nothing it did not already have. That argument is the whole justification, and it is why it does not extend to a remote origin, which has no filesystem access at all. allow-open-log-file and allow-get-app-url are left out on purpose rather than by oversight: the launcher's own splash and failure screens call them over the Tauri protocol, which the default capability covers, and the application page calls neither. A command nobody calls from this origin does not need a grant on this origin.
